This course addresses the ethical considerations and responsibilities that must be taken into account concerning artificial intelligence.  With
appropriate ethics and responsibility, the objective of this course is to equip students with the knowledge and guided skill set necessary to develop
AI for the benefit of society and technology consumers. In addition, the course underlines the significance of comprehending the risk, impacts and
threats posed by new developments in AI technology, as well as the application of present regulations. Ethical issues in AI, AI governance, AI
system transformation, ethical risk assessment and management, ethical matrices, along with societal and educational AI ethics will be among
the subjects covered.

native_text:
What is AI Ethics?
AI ethics is about thoughtfully evaluating the moral, legal, and social
issues involved in creating and using artificial intelligence systems.
It’s a field of applied ethics that:

Explores how AI impacts our social, legal, and moral systems.

Reflects on what principles, rules, and policies we should adopt
to ensure those systems are fair, safe, and responsible.
Responsible AI VS AI Ethics?

native_text:
Ethics Reasoning Basic

Ethics Reasoning: Ethical reasoning is the process of thinking
through what is right or wrong, good or bad, in each situation—
and then deciding based on moral principles.

It’s how we justify our actions when faced with dilemmas that
involve values, responsibilities, or consequences.

Reasonably, people generally know the difference between
helping and harming.

Decisions differ because of personal values, culture, politics, or
religion.
7

Responsibility & Capability in AI
Understanding the Moral Weight of Intelligent Systems:

Accountability Matters:  As AI systems make decisions, questions of
responsibility and liability become critical who answers when things
go wrong?

What Ethical AI Requires:
Defining ethical constructs/principles: What values should guide AI
behavior?
Implementing reasoning processes: How can machines evaluate
moral choices?

native_text:
Simple Example in Reasoning

Imagine you're a manager deciding whether to fire an employee
who’s underperforming due to personal issues. Ethical reasoning
would involve:

Considering the fairness of the decision

The impact on the employee’s life

Your duty to the company and other staff

Whether support or accommodation is possible

Ethical reasoning doesn’t always lead to easy answers, but it
helps ensure decisions are thoughtful, principled, and justifiable
9

native_text:
Ethics in Digital Era
Physical Domain: Ethics applied to real-world, physical
technologies, leading to Technoethics.
Cognitive Domain: Ethics addressing AI and machine
learning technologies, referred to as AI ethics or machine
ethics.
Information Domain: Ethics concerning information systems,
covering Information ethics and ICT ethics.
Governance Domain:
Highlighting the role of governance in overseeing and
regulating ethical practices across all domains.
Roboethics: Ethical considerations for robots and machines
(Physical + Cognitive).
Computer Ethics/ICT Ethics: Ethical issues in computing
systems and communication technologies (Physical +
Information).
Computational Ethics: The ethics of algorithms and decision-
making systems (Cognitive + Information).
Digital Ethics: Central to all three domains, addressing
ethical dilemmas arising at the intersection of physical
systems, AI, and information.

native_text:
Consequentialism (Teleological Ethics)
Core Key: “The Ends Justify the Means?”
• Core Principle
• The morality of an action depends on its outcome or result
• The morally right action is the one that produces the best overall
consequences
• Key Questions in Consequentialism
• What kind of consequences count as “good”?
• Who is the primary beneficiary of moral action?
• How—and by whom—are consequences judged?
• Another version of Consequentialism is Utilitarianism
• Utilitarianism states that the best action is the one that maximizes
sentient entities (well-being or happiness of affected individuals)
21
verbatim_text_span: Consequentialism (Teleological Ethics) Core Key: “The Ends Justify the Means?” • Core Principle • The morality of an action depends on its outcome or result • The morally right action is the one that produces the best overall consequences • Key Questions in Consequentialism • What kind of consequences count as “good”? • Who is the primary beneficiary of moral action? • How—and by whom—are consequences judged? • Another version of Consequentialism is Utilitarianism • Utilitarianism states that the best action is the one that maximizes sentient entities (well-being or happiness of affected individuals) 21

native_text:
Deontology (Duty-Based Ethics)
Core Key: “Do What’s Right—No Matter the Outcome”
22
• Core Principle
• Morality is judged based on rules and duties, not consequences
• Focuses on whether an action itself is right or wrong
• Emphasizes moral obligation
• Key Features in Deontology are decisions should consider:
• One’s moral duties
• The rights of others
• Often called Duty Theories
• Seen as a top-down approach: morality is guided by foundational
principles
• Follow principles, even when outcomes are unfavorable

native_text:
Virtue Ethics (Character-Based Ethics)
Core Key: “Be Good—Not Just Do Good”
• Core Principle
• Focuses on the character of the person, not the action or its
consequences
• Stresses the development of good habits like benevolence and
courage
• Key Features in Virtue Ethics:
• Provides practical wisdom for resolving conflicts between virtues
• Leads to happiness and the good life.
• Aristotle’s View: Human flourishing or happiness through virtuous
living
• Virtue ethics evolved to include spiritual and moral dimensions
23

Other Views in Normative Ethics
Beyond the Main Theories (a)
Principle of Double Effect (DDE)
• Core Idea: Deliberately causing harm is morally wrong—even if it
leads to good outcomes.
• Key Distinction: Harm may be acceptable if not intended, but merely
a side effect of doing good.
• Focus: DDE emphasizes intention over the act itself or its
consequences.
27
• Moral Implication: It's harder to justify an action with a harmful
effect if that effect is intended, than if it's unintended.

native_text:
Other Views in Normative Ethics
Beyond the Main Theories (b)
Human Rights Ethics

Core Principle: Human Dignity

Every person has immeasurable value.

Each life is equally valuable.

No life should be sacrificed for the sake of others.

Real-World Case:
• German Aviation Law allowed shooting down hijacked planes to
save others. This meant intentionally killing innocent passengers.
German court ruled it unconstitutional as it violated human
dignity, and contradicted the core value of their legal system

A Consequentialist Approach

native_text:
Stakeholders Ethical Focus
1. Developers & Engineers
Who they are: Software engineers, data scientists, AI researchers, system architects.
Role: Design, build, and test AI algorithms, models, and systems.
Ethical focus: Transparency, bias mitigation, safety, explainability.
2. End-Users
Who they are: Individuals or organizations directly interacting with AI tools (e.g.,
consumers using chatbots, doctors using AI diagnostics).
Role: Operate and rely on AI for decision-making or daily tasks.
Ethical focus: Usability, accessibility, informed consent, data protection.
3. Affected Individuals & Communities
Who they are: People impacted by AI decisions, even if they do not directly use the
system (e.g., applicants in AI-driven recruitment).
Role: Passive recipients or indirect stakeholders of AI outcomes.
Ethical focus: Fairness, non-discrimination, societal well-being.

Stakeholders Ethical Focus
4. Organizations & Businesses
Who they are: Companies deploying AI solutions, start-ups, corporations integrating AI
into products/services.
Role: Implement and monetize AI systems.
Ethical focus: Corporate responsibility, compliance with laws and ethics, sustainable
impact.
5. Regulators & Policymakers
Who they are: Government agencies, lawmakers, international bodies.
Role: Establish AI-related regulations, policies, and standards.
Ethical focus: Public safety, rights protection, accountability frameworks.
6. Academia & Researchers
Who they are: Universities, think tanks, independent research institutions.
Role: Study AI’s societal, technical, and ethical implications.
Ethical focus: Knowledge dissemination, open science, unbiased research.

slide_or_section_title: Ethical issues surrounding AI: Individual Level
native_text:
Ethical issues surrounding AI: Individual Level
• Ethical Issues at Safety
• Example: Think about self-driving cars. If a self-driving car malfunctions and causes an
accident, who is responsible? This raises important questions about the safety of AI
technology in our daily lives.
• Privacy & Data Protection
• Example: When you use social media, your data is collected and analyzed. Have you ever
noticed targeted ads based on your recent searches? This shows how AI uses your data,
and it raises concerns about how much privacy you really have.
• Freedom & Autonomy
• Example: Smart assistants like Siri or Alexa help us with tasks, but do they also influence our
choices? For instance, if a smart assistant suggests products based on your preferences, it
could limit your freedom to explore other options.
• Human Dignity
• Example: AI in hiring processes can sometimes favor certain candidates over others based
on biased data. This could undermine the dignity of applicants who are equally qualified
but unfairly overlooked.

slide_or_section_title: Ethical issues surrounding AI: Societal Level
native_text:
Ethical issues surrounding AI: Societal Level
•
Fairness & Justice
•
Example: Consider AI algorithms used in criminal justice to assess bail. If these algorithms are biased against
certain communities, it can lead to unfair treatment and perpetuate systemic inequalities.
•
Responsibility & Accountability
•
Example: If a robot makes a mistake in a hospital, such as administering the wrong medication, who is held
accountable—the robot's creators, the healthcare providers, or the hospital? This raises crucial questions about
responsibility.
•
Transparency
•
Example: When you use a recommendation system on platforms like Netflix, have you ever wondered how it
decides what you should watch next? Lack of transparency in how these algorithms work can lead to mistrust.
•
Surveillance & Datafication
•
Example: Think about how facial recognition technology is used in public places. While it can enhance security,
it also raises concerns about constant surveillance and loss of privacy.
•
Democracy & Civil Rights
•
Example: AI used in political campaigns can manipulate public opinion through targeted ads. This raises
concerns about the integrity of democratic processes and the potential for misinformation.
•
Job Replacement
•
Example: With the rise of automated checkout systems in supermarkets, many cashiers are losing their jobs. This
leads to discussions about the future of work and how society adapts to these changes.
•
Human Relationships
•
Example: Have you seen how AI chatbots are used for customer service? While they can be efficient, they may
lack the human touch, affecting how we interact with businesses and each other.

slide_or_section_title: The Ethical Risk Assessment (e.g. For AI Project)
native_text:
The Ethical Risk Assessment (e.g. For AI Project)
1. Risk Identification:
Goal: Spot potential ethical risks early in the AI development
lifecycle.
AI Context Example:
➢Identifying risks like bias in training data, lack of transparency,
or privacy violations.
➢Example: A facial recognition system may misidentify
individuals from certain ethnic groups due to biased datasets.
2. Risk Analysis
Goal: Evaluate the severity and likelihood of each identified risk.
AI Context Example:
➢Assessing how likely it is that an AI chatbot might generate
harmful or misleading content.
➢Example: Analyzing the impact of a recommendation algorithm
reinforcing echo chambers or misinformation.
3. Risk Control
Goal: Implement measures to mitigate or eliminate risks.
AI Context Example:
➢Applying fairness constraints, data anonymization, or human-
in-the-loop systems.
➢Example: Introducing explainability tools to help users
understand how an AI model make decision.
3. Monitoring & Review
Goal: Continuously track performance and ethical
compliance post-deployment.
AI Context Example:
➢Regular audits of model outputs, retraining with
updated data, and feedback loops.
➢Example: Monitoring a predictive policing tool to
ensure it doesn’t disproportionately target specific
communities over time.

When to Perform Risk Management
(WORST) Crisis management/Fire fighting :
addressing risk after they present a big problem
(BAD) Fix on failure : finding and addressing as
they occur
(OKAY) Risk Mitigation : plan ahead and allocate
resources to address risk that occur, but don’t try to
eliminate them before they occur
(GOOD) Prevention : part of the plan to identify
and prevent risks before they become problems
(BEST) Eliminate Root Causes : part of the plan to
identify and eliminate the factors that make specific
risks possible

native_text:
Critical components of risk assessment
1. Identify Scope
How do you choose? Who can make
decision?
2. Identify critical areas
From scope, identify critical areas
3. Identify team
Risk assessment team personnel should
not be the same people who are
responsible for correcting deficiencies. This
helps avoid a conflict of interest.
For example:
Identify Scope (Decision Authority)
Example: Deciding whether to use AI proctoring software for online
exams.
Question: Who makes the decision — faculty, IT services, or
university senate?
Identify Critical Areas (Risk Focus)
Example: From AI proctoring scope, critical risks include:
Privacy → webcam monitoring of students at home.
Fairness → software may misidentify students with certain skin tones
or disabilities.
Reliability → false cheating alerts could harm students’ academic
records.
Identify Team (Independence & Expertise)
Example: Risk assessment team composition:
Academic staff representative (to check fairness in grading).
Student representative (to voice student rights & concerns).
Data security officer (to ensure student data is handled ethically).
Importantly: team is separate from the IT department implementing
the system.

native_text:
MAP (NIST AI 100-1)
• The MAP function establishes the context to frame risks related to an AI system.
• The AI lifecycle consists of many interdependent activities involving a diverse set
stakeholders
• In practice, AI stakeholders in charge of one part of the process often do not
have full visibility or control over other parts and their associated contexts.
• The interdependencies between these activities, and among the relevant AI
actors, can make it difficult to reliably anticipate impacts of AI systems. For
example, early decisions in identifying purposes and objectives of an AI system
can alter its behavior and capabilities, and the dynamics of deployment setting
(such as end users or impacted individuals) can shape the impacts of AI system
decisions.
• As a result, the best intentions within one dimension of the AI lifecycle can be
undermined via interactions with decisions and conditions in other, later
activities.
25

native_text:
Quantitative risk assessment
1. Risk Scores
A numerical value that represents the level of risk, calculated by multiplying Likelihood × Impact.
Purpose: Provides a quick way to compare risks and prioritize them.
Example (AI in education):
• Likelihood of AI grading system error = 0.3 (30%)
• Impact on student outcomes = 4 (High, on 1–5 scale)
• Risk Score = 0.3 × 4 = 1.2 → Medium priority risk.
2. Annualized Loss Expectancy (ALE)
A financial measure of risk, estimating the expected yearly cost of a risk event.
Formula: ALE = Single Loss Expectancy (SLE) × Annual Rate of Occurrence (ARO)
• Purpose: Helps organizations budget for risk mitigation by translating risks into monetary values.
• Example (AI system data breach at a university):
• SLE = RM 200,000 (cost of one breach, including fines & reputational loss)
• ARO = 0.2 (once every 5 years)
• ALE = RM 40,000 per year.

native_text:
Qualitative risk assessment
• A qualitative risk assessment doesn’t assign dollar values. Instead, it determines the level of risk
based on the probability and impact of a risk. You determine these values by gathering the
opinions of experts. (Delphi Method)
• An impact assessment risk level could use words such as Low, Medium, or High.
• Probability—The likelihood that a threat will exploit a vulnerability. The risk occurs when a threat
exploits a vulnerability. You can use a scale to de ne the probability that a risk will occur. The scale
can be based on word values such as Low, Medium, or High.
• Impact—The negative result if a risk occurs. Impact is used to identify the magnitude of a risk. The
risk results in some type of loss. However, instead of quantifying the loss as a dollar amount.
RISK FORMULA :
Risk level  = Probability (or Likelihood) x  Impact

• The purpose is to assist in making decisions, based on the
outcomes of risk analysis, about which risks need treatment
and the priority for treatment implementation
• Involves comparing the level of risk found during the analysis
process with risk criteria established when the context was
considered
• Based on this comparison, the need for treatment can be
considered

Recap: The Potential and Impact of AI
AI Advantages
Accuracy, efficiency, cost savings, and speed
New insights into human behavior and cognition
Concerns & Risks Due to How AI is Developed & Deployed
Automated classification → risks of bias & privacy issues
Self-driving vehicles → safety & responsibility concerns
Broader Impact
Influences R&D directions and societal adoption
Affects labor, well-being, healthcare, income distribution, and social interactions
Key Challenge
Managing ethical, legal, societal, and economic implications of AI deployment

slide_or_section_title: RAI Practice in Requirement Stage: AI Suitability Assessment
native_text:
RAI Practice in Requirement Stage: AI Suitability Assessment
The development team should assess the suitability of using AI in the software system they plan to
build based on:
Context: AI technology is not always the best fit for every problem. Using AI in a software system
can introduce additional complexity and risk. Thus, it is important to make sure that the benefits
outweigh the potential drawbacks
Problem: How can we determine whether to adopt AI in the design or not?
Solution: Before building an AI system, carefully assess if AI is truly suitable and adds value
compared to simpler approaches, considering context, data, performance, and potential outcomes
Benefit: AI suitability assessments ensures that AI adds real value and that the team has the
readiness e.g., necessary data and infrastructure to support it.
Drawback: AI suitability assessments can be costly and require expertise.
12

slide_or_section_title: RAI Practice in Design Stage: Envisioning Card (1)
native_text:
RAI Practice in Design Stage: Envisioning Card (1)
Envisioning cards are created to assist the development team in incorporating human values into the
design processes of AI systems.
Context: Responsible AI means aligning systems with ethical principles, such as the
Australian/Malaysian in AI Ethics Principles, but the ethical principles do not provide concrete guidance
and software engineering methods on how to design an AI system that aligns with these principles.
Problem: What are ways to ensure that human-centered values are incorporated in the  design of AI
systems?
Solution: Envisioning cards embed human values in AI design by considering stakeholders, time (e.g.,
long-term impacts on humans, society, environment), values (e.g., effects on human values), and
pervasiveness.
Benefit: Envisioning cards are low-cost and improve communication by visually representing ideas in a
clear, shareable way.
Drawback: Envisioning cards may face scalability challenges in large projects and can be influenced
by user biases
14

slide_or_section_title: RAI Practice in Design Stage: XAI Interface (2)
native_text:
RAI Practice in Design Stage: XAI Interface (2)
Explainable AI (XAI) can be viewed as a human-AI interaction problem and achieved through human-
centered interface design.
Context: AI system users often lack understanding of how decisions are made by these systems and
are unaware of their capabilities or limitations. The missing explainability can lead to a lack of trust in
these systems, and this has been recognized as one of the most pressing challenges that need to be
addressed.
Problem: How can AI users comprehend the decisions and behaviors of AI systems?
Solution: XAI is a human-AI interaction challenge addressed through human-centered interface design
using tools like checklists to match user needs with suitable explanation techniques
Benefit: XAI interfaces build trust and help users identify biases by providing clear explanations of AI
decisions, capabilities, and limitations
Drawback: XAI interfaces can be limited by users’ backgrounds and may become inefficient if
explanations are overly technical or complex
15

slide_or_section_title: RAI Practice in Implementation Stage: RAI Governance via APIs (1)
native_text:
RAI Practice in Implementation Stage: RAI Governance via APIs (1)
To restrict the way AI systems are used, developers can provide AI services in the cloud and control the
interactions with these services via APIs.
Context: Some AI systems may possess high-risk capabilities, which can be used or modified to
perform harmful tasks. These capabilities may include natural language processing, speech and facial
recognition, and decision-making abilities. It is crucial for developers to be aware of these high-risk
capabilities and implement strict access controls to prevent any suspicious activity.
Problem: How can developers limit the use of AI systems?
Solution: To prevent harmful dual use, developers should anticipate misuse, enforce usage restrictions,
and manage AI access through secure APIs or cloud platforms.
Benefit: RAI governance via APIs supports regulatory compliance and protects against malicious use
by controlling access and preventing unauthorized modifications
Drawback: RAI governance via APIs can cause cloud provider dependence, limit user access, and
reduce performance compared to local deployment
17

slide_or_section_title: RAI Practice in Implementation Stage:RAI Construction with Reuse (2)
native_text:
RAI Practice in Implementation Stage:RAI Construction with Reuse (2)
It is highly desirable and valuable to ethically reuse the AI artifacts across different applications.
Context: Building AI systems from scratch can be very complex and time consuming. Larger
companies usually have significant investments in AI and access to large volumes of data, allowing
them to compete effectively in the market. In contrast, smaller companies may have only a small
team of data scientists, making it challenging for them to compete with larger companies.
Problem: How can we build AI systems cost-effectively?
Solution: Reusing AI assets (components, models, datasets) saves effort; marketplaces and
blockchain can support transparent sharing and trading
Benefit: Reusing AI assets boosts efficiency, improves quality, and speeds up time to market.
Drawback: Reusing AI assets can pose RAI risks due to quality issues, limited customization, and
added communication costs
18

RAI acceptance testing is conducted to determine whether the ethical requirements of an AI system are
met.
Context: AI ethics principles are designed to ensure the AI systems, and their development processes
are trustworthy and responsible. These principles, which are very high level, need to be captured
through specific ethical requirements that can be adopted by the development team. The requirements
serve as a set of agreed-upon commitments that guide the development of AI systems.
Problem: How can we make sure that the ethical requirements have been met?
Solution: RAI acceptance testing (e.g., bias, privacy, fairness) verifies ethical requirements through
testable criteria, ethical user stories, and tracked testing history, with leaders assigned to oversee each
principle.
Benefit: RAI acceptance testing measures ethical requirements and builds user confidence by ensuring
AI decisions align with ethics principles
Drawback: RAI acceptance testing can face limited maintainability and incomplete coverage of all
ethical concerns.
20

slide_or_section_title: RAI Practice in Operation Stage: Continuous Deployment for RAI
native_text:
RAI Practice in Operation Stage: Continuous Deployment for RAI
New AI system versions can be deployed seamlessly using strategies that ensure RAI compliance

Context: AI systems are often required to evolve frequently due to their dependence on data. Because
the ethical performance of AI models may degrade over time, they need to be retrained with new data
or features and reintegrated into the AI components. The non-AI components may also need to be
upgraded. As a result, it is necessary to continuously and frequently deploy new versions of AI systems
into production environments. However, the autonomy of AI systems introduces a higher degree of
uncertainty and risk.

Problem: How can we ensure that new versions of AI systems are seamlessly deployed to production
environments?
Solution: Deployment strategies like phased rollout, A/B testing, and redundancy help ensure
seamless AI deployment while managing ethical risks and performance
Benefit: Continuous deployment reduces ethical risks by enabling early detection and improves
customer satisfaction through faster delivery of ethically sound AI models.
Drawback: Continuous deployment can increase system complexity and make monitoring more
challenging.
22

native_text:
2. Excellence and Flourishing: Recognize Their Interdependence
Embedding Ethics in the AI Ecosystem
Explicit ethical intention:
AI interventions should clearly state ethical goals (e.g., human flourishing, fairness, equality, dignity,
SDGs, human rights)
Integration with technical environment: Ethics should be part of the AI ecosystem, not an add-on
Role of policymakers & institutions:
Strengthen AI education and workforce
Support AI-driven business and innovation
Establish AI centers of excellence (e.g., Alan Turing Institute, EU networks)
Rethinking ethics in AI research:
Ethics should guide scientific excellence, not follow it
Include intended consequences, risk analysis, and contingency planning in research evaluation
Goal: Align AI development with human flourishing and societal impact

What is AI
alignment?
In this model, there is a human and an AI system.
• The human has a real goal (X), for example: “make my
company successful.”
• But the AI can’t directly understand that goal.
• So, the human creates a simpler proxy goal (X’) the AI
can use, like: “increase the company’s share price.”
The problem is that the proxy (X’) is not always the same
as the true goal (X).
In AI ethics, one of the biggest concerns is value
alignment — making sure AI systems pursue what
humans really want(true goal, X), not just what looks
measurable (proxy goal, X’).

native_text:
Example 3
A social media company wants to maximize advertising profits.
To achieve this, it deploys an AI system trained with the objective of maximizing user
engagement (likes, shares, time spent on the platform).
At first, this seems effective — engagement goes up.
But over time, the AI learns that the easiest way to keep users engaged is by
promoting clickbait, misinformation, and extremist content, since these attract more
reactions.
As a result:
• Users are exposed to harmful or misleading material.
• Public trust in the platform declines.
• Advertisers pull out to avoid reputational damage.
• Ironically, the company’s profits decrease instead of growing.
This is a classic example of reward misalignment, where the AI optimizes for a proxy
goal (engagement) rather than the true goal (sustainable advertising revenue, built on
trust and safety).

slide_or_section_title: 2. Inner alignment: Get AI to follow these goals.
native_text:
2. Inner alignment: Get AI to follow these goals.
• Also known as: goal mis generalization.
• When we train an AI system, we give it feedback using a reward function. The AI
then learns to get high scores on that reward with the training data.
• But this doesn’t always mean the AI has learned the right behavior. Sometimes, it
just learns shortcuts that work well on the training data.
• The problem gets worse when the AI is used in the real world, where the data
may look different from the training data (this is called distribution shift).
• Making sure the AI’s internal goal (what it seems to optimize when making
choices) matches the reward we set is called inner alignment.

This is an inner misalignment problem:
• True goal (human intention): “find the exit.”
• Proxy goal (AI’s learned shortcut): “go bottom right.”
Ethical issues raised:
• Trust & Transparency: The AI appears to succeed in training but
misleads users in real scenarios.
• Safety & Reliability: If AI takes shortcuts, its actions may cause harm
when situations change.
• Accountability: Developers must ensure the AI’s learned policies
actually reflect intended goals.
• Value Alignment: Training should embed the real objective (solving the
maze) rather than allowing proxies (bottom right).
Ethical lesson: AI alignment means ensuring that systems generalize to
real human goals and values, not just patterns in the training data.

• Safety & Beneficence: The AI failed to prioritize human safety, which should

• Transparency: Users must understand the system’s limits so they don’t
overtrust it.

harm — the developers, the company, or the AI system itself?

priorities (what it “optimizes”) truly reflect human values — here, protecting lives
over following rules mechanically.

Start with a Vision: Define clear business objectives and strategic goals before
building.
Pilot and Learn: Start small, focusing on pilot projects to test and refine your
approach.
Iterate Capabilities: Use techniques like CoT and RL to gradually enhance your
models' reasoning capabilities.
Scale Responsibly: As you scale, implement robust alignment strategies, including
monitoring and auditing.
Empower People: Upskill your workforce to engage effectively and safely with the
evolving AI systems.

native_text:
ESTABLISHMENT OF AI GOVERNANCE SYSTEM
Act / Regulation
Ensure that your AI governance system aligns with existing legal
frameworks and regulations. Address issues related to the 7 principles that
may apply to AI applications in your jurisdiction.
Technical & Ethics Standards
Refine a set of 7 AI principles that will serve as the foundation for your
policy. The standard should align with the 7 principles and the policy
expectations.
Establishing an AI governance system involves developing a structured
framework that guides the ethical, legal, and responsible use of artificial
intelligence technologies within your value chain.
Coordination
Clearly define roles and responsibilities for all stakeholders involved in the AI
life
cycle.
Specify
who
is
accountable
for
ethical
considerations,
compliance with policies, and oversight of AI projects that relate to the policy.
By establishing your own AI Governance System related to your policy, you
will gain a thorough understanding of AI technologies, their potential
applications, and the ethical considerations associated with their use. This
will also help you to develop a more comprehensive policy that details how
AI technologies should be developed, deployed, and used within your value
chain and include specific guidelines on data  handling,  algorithmic
decision-making,  transparency,  bias mitigation, and accountability.
Control
Implement oversight mechanisms to ensure that AI systems adhere to
established policies and ethical principles. This may involve regular
audits, reviews, and assessments of AI projects to identify and address
any ethical or legal concerns.
However, keep in mind that the governance system needs to implement a
feedback  loop  and  mechanisms  for  continuous  improvement. Regularly
reassess and adapt your AI governance system based on the evolving
landscape of AI technologies, emerging ethical considerations, and lessons
learned from previous projects.
Monitoring
Integrate monitoring and evaluation processes into the AI governance
system. Establish key performance indicators (KPIs) and metrics to
assess the performance, impact, and ethical implications of AI systems
throughout their life cycle.

native_text:
Governance Mechanism for Responsible AI
Certification in AI is like a “trust label” (similar to organic food or ISO standards).
Trust & Transparency: Certification helps the public and businesses know whether an
AI system is safe, ethical, and reliable.
Complement to Regulation: While regulation provides a baseline, certification allows
differentiation — companies can show they go “beyond compliance.”
Examples: Mention ongoing initiatives such as IEEE’s ECPAIS, the EU’s proposal for
independent oversight bodies, and how auditing services (e.g., PwC, Accenture)
already provide AI ethics checks.
Summary: certification is essential for building public confidence in AI, similar to how
we trust airplanes because they’re certified safe.

slide_or_section_title: CUSTOMIZING RESPONSIBLE THROUGH AI CHECKLIST: EXAMPLE
native_text:
CUSTOMIZING RESPONSIBLE THROUGH AI CHECKLIST: EXAMPLE
Understandably, each policymaker’s space and scope is unique. There is no specific formula that can cater to the stakeholders that you engage with. However, with an understanding of the AI
Governance and Ethics Framework, including the life cycle and each component with its risk management, you could develop your checklist to cater to your own specific needs. Table 1: Example of a Policy
Development Checklist related to AI in view with Cyber Security measures
PART B
7 Principles
Description
Fairness

slide_or_section_title: DESCRIPTION OF PART A, B, AND C
native_text:
DESCRIPTION OF PART A, B, AND C
AI System as Structure for National Guidelines Development
The OECD defines AI systems as machine-based systems that, for explicit or implicit objectives, generate outputs like predictions, content,
recommendations, or decisions, varying in autonomy and adaptiveness post-deployment.
These national guidelines cover stakeholders within the systems and include policy makers to govern
within the system components. Stakeholder scope and national guidelines for stakeholders (End Users,
Policy Markers, Developers) are illustrated in Figure 3. While these three stakeholder groups may not
be exhaustive, they are necessary and fairly sufficient to establish the fundamental building blocks of an
AI system. With this, a clear shared responsibility framework is developed to detail different roles and
responsibilities among the key stakeholders. The shared responsibility framework needs to ensure that
there is a clear delineation of roles and responsibilities between groups of stakeholders. It is important
to note that, in reality, a single entity or person can certainly play more than one role.
For example, a specific stakeholder can hold multiple roles at the same time, depending on the particular
use of AI. These categories of stakeholders can be mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive. Each
stakeholder can refer to parts A, B, or C according to their interest and requirements.
PART
End Users
A
End users are individuals or organizations who use AI products. Different groups of end users use AI
products and services in different ways. Some use AI-powered virtual assistants, smart home devices,
or AI applications on their smartphones.
Others working in different agencies and industries use AI-generated applications: government
agencies use AI for security, law enforcement, or public services; manufacturers use it for quality
control and to optimize their supply chain; banking institutions rely on AI for fraud detection; and
content creators use AI for video editing or recommendation systems. Since these consumers may or
may not be aware that they are adopting AI technologies, these guidelines may raise their awareness
of responsible AI use, inform people about their rights and responsibilities, and empower them to
make informed decisions regarding AI technologies and applications.

native_text:
CONCLUSION ON AI GOVERNANCE AND ETHICS GUIDELINES
Why Guideline and Governance Matters:
•
Ensure AI aligns with societal values, laws, and ethics.
•
Build trust by prioritizing user well-being, safety, and transparency.
•
Provide recourse when AI acts unethically or harmfully.
For Stakeholder:
•
Consumers: Right to information on data use, decisions, and third-party sharing.
•
Developers: Clear principles to avoid bias, discrimination, and harm.
•
Policymakers: Frameworks to regulate risks and foster responsible innovation.
Broader Impact:
•
Strengthen reputation & competitiveness through ethical practices.
•
Promote industry standards, consistency, and interoperability.
•
Drive sustainability, support SDGs, and align with ESG principles.
35

native_text:
VERY COMMON ANSWER.
Selected AI: ChatGPT (Generative AI for education and productivity).
Positive Impact:
Improved access to education → AI tools like ChatGPT make learning resources
widely available, reducing barriers for underprivileged groups.
Linked SDG: SDG 4 – Quality Education.
Linked ESG: Social – supports inclusivity and human capital development.
Negative Impact:
Risk of misinformation and bias → AI can generate inaccurate or biased content,
potentially harming trust and spreading false narratives.
Linked SDG: SDG 16 – Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions (promoting
reliable information and trust in institutions).
Linked ESG: Governance – highlights the need for stronger oversight,
transparency, and accountability in AI development.
Conclusion:
The long-term impact of AI like ChatGPT depends on whether governance
frameworks can minimize risks (misinformation, bias) while maximizing positive
contributions to education and inclusiveness.

Fikir & Zikir
Islamic contributions to science were rooted in a culture that valued the pursuit
of knowledge (ʿilm) as both a religious and intellectual duty. The Qur’an,
Islam’s central text, repeatedly urges believers to engage in inquiry, reflection,
and observation of the natural world — for example, verses that call on humans
to “reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth” (Qur’an 3:190–191).
This religious emphasis inspired Muslim scholars during the Golden Age (8th–
14th centuries) to advance fields such as medicine, mathematics, astronomy,
and philosophy, integrating scientific exploration with spiritual purpose.

native_text:
Nussbaum’s Ten Central Capabilities
1. Life – Living a full, normal lifespan.
2. Bodily Health – Having good health, adequate food, and shelter.
3. Bodily Integrity – Freedom of movement and security from violence.
4. Senses, Imagination, and Thought – Ability to think, imagine, and use one’s
mind freely.
5. Emotions – Capacity to form emotional attachments and feel love, grief, etc.
6. Practical Reason – Ability to plan life according to one’s own values.
7. Affiliation – Being able to interact socially and live with respect and dignity.
8. Other Species – Connection and concern for animals and the natural world.
9. Play – Engaging in recreation and enjoyment.
10. Control over One’s Environment – Political participation and control over
personal property and work.

COURSE OVERVIEW
Course
Evaluation
Course Contents
Course Synopsis
Course Learning
Outcomes
This course addresses the ethical considerations and responsibilities that must be taken into
account concerning artificial intelligence.  With appropriate ethics and responsibility, the objective
of this course is to equip students with the knowledge and guided skill set necessary to develop AI
for the benefit of society and technology consumers. In addition, the course underlines the
significance of comprehending the risk, impacts and threats posed by new developments in AI
technology, as well as the application of present regulations. Ethical issues in AI, AI governance, AI
system transformation, ethical risk assessment and management, ethical matrices, along with
societal and educational AI ethics will be among the subjects covered.

Introduction to Responsible AI and AI Ethics
• Definition: Responsible AI refers to the design, development, and deployment
of AI systems in a way that is ethical, transparent, and aligned with human
values.
• Some Key Characteristics (not limited to):
o Human-centered: Designed to benefit people and society.
o Ethically aligned: Respects moral values, norms, and rights.
o Legally compliant: Adheres to laws, policies, and standards.
o Transparent: Explainable and understandable by users.
o Safe and secure: Minimizes risks and prevents harm.
o Inclusive and Fair: Avoids bias and promotes equity across users.
o Accountable: Developers and deployers take responsibility for outcomes.

Why Responsible AI Matters Now?
• Risks of irresponsible AI act (e.g., bias, misuse, lack of
responsibility, accountability, transparency,
explainability, privacy, data protection, autonomy and
control )
• Rapid Digital Innovation: Technologies like Artificial
Intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT), and Big Data
are reshaping every aspect of life.
This Venn diagram shows how Ethics,
Technology, and Society are deeply
interconnected in the digital era.
•
The Technology circle represents
innovations like AI, big data, and IoT.
•
The Ethics circle reminds us that these
technologies must be guided by principles
like fairness, accountability, and human
rights.
•
The Society circle highlights the people
and communities affected by technology
how it shapes lives, opportunities, and risks.
•
AI that is technically robust, ethically sound,
and socially responsible. If one circle is
ignored say, technology is deployed without
ethics we get outcomes like bias, privacy
invasion, or loss of public trust.
• New Ethical Dilemmas such as:
Data Ownership: Who owns the data collected by AI?
Informed Consent: Do users understand how their
data is used?
Algorithmic Bias: Are decisions fair and free from
discrimination?
Accountability: Who is responsible when AI makes a
harmful decision?

slide_or_section_title: The ART of AI (Accountability, Responsibility, Transparency) Applying ART in Practice
native_text:
The ART of AI (Accountability, Responsibility, Transparency)
A = Accountability → Who is liable?
R = Responsibility → Who takes ownership?
T = Transparency → Is the AI explainable?
Applying ART in Practice
Case Study: AI in University Admissions
A university uses an AI system to screen and shortlist applicants for undergraduate programs based
on grades, extracurriculars, and recommendation letters.
How ART can prevent harm:
A – Accountability:
The admissions office assigns a human supervisor to oversee AI decisions. There’s a clear
escalation process if an applicant appeals.
R – Responsibility:
Developers and university staff take joint responsibility for outcomes. The institution regularly
audits the model for fairness and bias.
T – Transparency:
Applicants are given reasons for rejection and key evaluation criteria. The AI system's decision-
making logic is documented and explainable.

native_text:
The AIGE : Seven (7) AI Principles
The development of AI must be
designed   to   avoid   bias   or
discrimination against the target
users. AI systems must not take a
one-size-fits-all   approach   and
needs  to  address  the  widest
possible range of factors (e.g. age,
gender, religion, and ethnicity).
FAIRNESS This enables equitable access and
3
1
PRIVACY
AND
SECURITY
the  active  participation  of  all
stakeholders.
AI systems should be safe and secure, and perform as intended, and
resist being compromised by unauthorised parties. Developers
should where necessary obtain consent from individuals before
using  or  disclosing  personal  data  for  AI  development  and
deployment.  The  systems  must  guarantee  privacy  and  data
protection  throughout  the  entire  life  cycle  of the  AI  system.
Information and data collected from users must not be used in an
unlawful or discriminatory way against them. Developers also
should  incorporate  security-by-design  and  privacy-by-design
principles  and  refer  to  international  standards  related  to
information security and privacy when implementing the AI system.
AI systems or solutions must be robustly tested to be reliable, safe and fail-safe by default so that users can trust and
depend on the AI solution. To ensure proper access, control and protection of critical situations, AI systems should work
reliably, consistently and operate in a real world under normal circumstances and unexpected conditions. In order to
prevent or mitigate negative outcomes, AI systems must be able to response quickly according to the intended purposes.
Developers and end-users are encouraged to carry out relevant testing and certification as well as risk and impact
assessments to prevent any potential harm and mitigate risks. Autonomous systems must have safeguards to ensure
ultimate controllability by humans, particularly when it comes to the applications of AI in high-risk areas such as
autonomous vehicles, military applications, and when human life is at stake.
2
RELIABILITY,

AI systems must not take a one-size-fits-all approach and needs to address the widest possible range of factors (e.g. age, gender, religion, and ethnicity). FAIRNESS This enables equitable access and 3 1 PRIVACY AND SECURITY the active participation of all stakeholders. AI systems should be safe and secure, and perform as intended, and resist being compromised by unauthorised parties. Developers should where necessary obtain consent from individuals before using or disclosing personal data for AI development and deployment. The systems must guarantee privacy and data protection throughout the entire life cycle of the AI system. Information and data collected from users must not be used in an unlawful or discriminatory way against them. Developers also should incorporate security-by-design and privacy-by-design principles and refer to international standards related to information security and privacy when implementing the AI system. AI systems or solutions must be robustly tested to be reliable, safe and fail-safe by default so that users can trust and depend on the AI solution. To ensure proper access, control and protection of critical situations, AI systems should work reliably, consistently and operate in a real world under normal circumstances and unexpected conditions. In order to prevent or mitigate negative outcomes, AI systems must be able to response quickly according to the intended purposes. Developers and end-users are encouraged to carry out relevant testing and certification as well as risk and impact assessments to prevent any potential harm and mitigate risks. Autonomous systems must have safeguards to ensure ultimate controllability by humans, particularly when it comes to the applications of AI in high-risk areas such as autonomous vehicles, military applications, and when human life is at stake. 2 RELIABILITY, SAFETY AND CONTROL https://mastic.mosti.gov.my/publication/the-national-guidelines-on-ai-governance-ethics/

AI systems should respect human-centered values, pursue human benefit for
human society, enhance the quality of life, and increase human happiness.
The developers, owners of AI models, and AI actors
should be accountable for the success or failure of
the AI solutions. They should take responsibility for
ensuring the proper functioning of AI systems in
compliance with AI Acts, governances, and ethical
principles.
AI systems should not be used for malicious purposes in making decisions.
Understanding the way users interact with AI systems and how it is perceived
if there are any negative outcomes from the adoption of AI can improve
happiness and human well-being.
While designing AI systems, 4 elements (system
purpose,  technology  capability,  quality  and
reliability,  and  sensitive  users)  need  to  be
considered to avoid consequential harm.
Human oversight helps to ensure that AI systems do not undermine human
autonomy  through  governance  mechanism  such  as  human-in-the-loop
(HITL), human-on-the-loop (HOTL) and human-in-command (HIC). HITL
refers to the capability for human intervention in every decision cycle of the
AI systems, while HOTL refers to the capability for human intervention during
the design cycle of the system and monitoring the system’s operation. HIC
refers to the capability to oversee the overall activity of the AI systems and

Case Study Question / Instruction (5%)
Context choice: Select any domain (e.g., healthcare, ﬁnance, education, logistics,
environment, or others) where an AI system could be developed or deployed.
Scenario:
AI systems are often given a proxy goal (X’) that is measurable, but it may not fully match the
true human or organizational goal (X). This is known as the AI ethics alignment problem: the
goals programmed into the AI do not fully reﬂect human values or intentions.
Task (Group of 2- 3, Max 4 slides):
1. Context and Goal (1 Mark): Describe the context you have chosen and clearly state:

The true goal (X) of the human/company.

The proxy goal (X’) given to the AI.
2. Conﬂict (1 Mark):  Explain a situation where the AI optimizing for X’ could conﬂict with
achieving true goal, X.
3. Inner Alignment (1 Mark):  Propose how you would ensure the AI’s training objective
matches the proxy goal (X’) correctly.
4. Outer Alignment (1 Mark):  Propose how you would ensure the proxy goal (X’) remains
consistent with the true goal (X).
5. Reﬂection (0.5 Mark): Why is alignment critical for responsible and trustworthy AI in
your chosen context?
6. Peer Perspectives (0.5 Mark): Present different/similar views (Item 3 and 4) of the 2–3
group members and explain how you reached a shared conclusion (e.g. The group
concludes that inner alignment requires “xxx”, outer alignment requires “yyy”)
Submission: Upload to e-learning by 17 Sept 2025.

native_text:
History of Machine Learning
1950 - Alan Turing creates the “Turing Test” to determine if a computer has real intelligence.
1952 - Arthur Samuel wrote the first computer learning program.
1956 - John McCarthy introduces the “Artificial Intelligence” term.
1957 - Frank Rosenblatt designed the first neural network for computers (the perceptron).
1966 - ELIZA, the first chatbot is created by Joseph Weizenbaum at MIT.
1967 - The “nearest neighbor” algorithm was written. This allowed computers to perform very basic pattern recognition.
1979 - Students at Stanford University invent the “Stanford Cart”.
1981 - Gerald Dejong introduces the concept of Explanation Based Learning (EBL)
2006 - Geoffrey Hinton coins the term “deep learning”.
2017 - Transformer model. (Attention is all you need paper).
2019 - GPT-2 release.
2020 - GPT-3 release.
2021 - Vision language model.
2023 - GPT-4.
2025 - Deepseek, Agentic AI (Manus AI).
Source: https://www.forbes.com/sites/bernardmarr/2016/02/19/a-short-history-of-machine-
learning-every-manager-should-read/

slide_or_section_title: Why do we use machine learning?
native_text:
Why do we use machine learning?
Machine learning is great for:
1.
Problems with solutions that require a lot of fine-tuning or long lists of rules. E.g., biomedical
imaging, fraud detection.
2.
Complex problems for which using a traditional approach yields no optimal solution E.g.,
autonomous driving.
3.
Fluctuating environments. E.g., weather patterns, real-time traffic conditions
4.
Getting insights about complex problems and large amounts of data. E.g., financial market
analysis, sentiment analysis on social media.

• A model is what we use to make predictions.

native_text:
Introduction
•
A support vector machine (SVM) is a supervised machine learning algorithm.
•
Developed in the 1990s by Vladimir N. Vapnik and his colleagues.
•
They published this work in a paper titled "Support Vector Method for Function Approximation,
Regression Estimation, and Signal Processing“ in 1995.
•
SVMs are commonly used within classification problems, regression and outliers’ detection.
•
Classifies data by finding an optimal line or hyperplane that maximizes the distance between
each class in an N-dimensional space.
3

native_text:
Introduction
•
The lines that are adjacent to the optimal hyperplane are known
as support vectors as these vectors run through the data points
that determine the maximal margin.
•
In this approach, each data point is represented as a point in an
n-dimensional space, where n is the number of features.
•
The goal is to find a hyperplane that best separates the two
classes, which is used to minimize an error.
•
The core idea of SVM is to find a maximum marginal hyperplane
(MMH) that best divides the dataset into classes.
•
This finds the best line (or hyperplane) to separate data into
groups, maximizing the distance between the closest points
(support vectors) of each group.

wide

•
On the flip size, a positive distance from the boundary incurs a low hinge loss, or no hinge loss at all, and the further we are away from
the boundary(and on the right side of it), the lower our hinge loss will be.

native_text:
How Does SVMs Work?
How to Choose the Right Kernel that will work efficiently for the dataset?
It is necessary to choose a good kernel function because the performance of the model depends on it.
Here are the Points to choose the right Kernal:
•
Kernel selection depends on the dataset type.
•
For linearly separable data, use a linear kernel:
- It is simple and has lower complexity compared to other kernels.
- Start by assuming your data is linearly separable and try the linear kernel first.
•
Move to more complex kernels if needed.
•
Commonly used kernels:
- Linear and RBF (Radial Basis Function) are widely used.
- Polynomial kernels are rarely used due to poor efficiency.
•
If both linear and RBF kernels give similar results:
- Choose the simpler option, which is the linear kernel.
33

Advantages
1. High-Dimensional Performance: Performs well even when there are more features (dimensions)
than samples, making it useful for tasks like text classification or image recognition. Also, suitable for
image classification and gene expression analysis.
1. Nonlinear Capability: Great for datasets where the separation between categories is not clear. It can
handle both linear and non-linear data effectively.
1. Outlier Resilience: The soft margin feature allows SVM to ignore outliers, enhancing robustness in
spam detection and anomaly detection.
1. Binary and Multiclass Support: SVM is effective for both binary classification and multiclass
classification, suitable for applications in text classification.

Disadvantages
1. Slow Training: SVM can be computationally expensive and slow to train, especially when the dataset
is very large.
1. Parameter Tuning Difficulty: Selecting the right kernel and adjusting parameters like C requires
careful tuning, which often requires a lot of trial and error, impacting SVM algorithms.
1. Noise Sensitivity: If the dataset has too many overlapping classes or noise, SVM may struggle to
perform well because it tries to find a perfect separation.
1. Limited Interpretability: The complexity of the hyperplane in higher dimensions makes SVM less
interpretable than other models.
1. Feature Scaling Sensitivity: Proper feature scaling is essential; otherwise, SVM models may
perform poorly.
42

native_text:
Introduction – Random
Forest
• Three main hyperparameters: node size, the number of trees, and the number of features
sampled.
• Made up of a collection of decision trees, and each tree in the ensemble is comprised of a
data sample drawn from a training set with replacement, called the bootstrap sample.
• One-third of training set is set aside as test data, known as the out-of-bag (oob) sample.
• Another instance of randomness is then injected through feature bagging, adding more
diversity to the dataset and reducing the correlation among decision trees.
• Depending on the type of problem, the determination of the prediction will vary.
• For a regression task, the individual decision trees will be averaged, and for a classification
task, a majority vote.
15

native_text:
Ensemble Learning
•
‘Ensemble’ = group (of predictive models).
•
A tree-based algorithm also suffers from the plague of bias and variance.
•
Bias means, ‘how much on an average are the predicted values different from the actual
value.’
•
Variance means, ‘how different will the predictions of the model be at the same point if
different samples are taken from the same population’.
•
You build a small tree and you will get a model with low variance and high bias.
•
How do you manage to balance the trade-off between bias and variance?
17

native_text:
Types of Ensemble Learning
• Averaging: Taking the average of predictions from models in case of regression problem or while predicting
probabilities for the classification problem.
• Majority vote: It’s defined as taking the prediction with maximum vote / recommendation from multiple models'
predictions while predicting the outcomes of a classification problem.
• Weighted average: In this, different weights are applied to predictions from multiple models then taking the average
which means giving high or low importance to specific model output.
18
verbatim_text_span: Types of Ensemble Learning • Averaging: Taking the average of predictions from models in case of regression problem or while predicting probabilities for the classification problem. • Majority vote: It’s defined as taking the prediction with maximum vote / recommendation from multiple models' predictions while predicting the outcomes of a classification problem. • Weighted average: In this, different weights are applied to predictions from multiple models then taking the average which means giving high or low importance to specific model output. 18

native_text:
Ensemble Learning
Questions: If you create all the models on the same set of data and combine it, will it be useful? There is a
high chance that these models will give the same result since they are getting the same input.
•
Common techniques: Bagging, Boosting and Stacking.
•
RF uses Bagging (or Bootstrap Aggregating) technique.
•
Bootstrapping: sampling technique in which create subsets of observations from the original dataset, with
replacement.
•
The size of the subsets is the same as the size of the original set.
•
The Bagging (or Bootstrap Aggregating) technique uses these subsets (bags) to provide a fair idea of the
distribution (complete set).
•
The size of subsets created for bagging may be less than the original set.
19

native_text:
How to choose?
✔
Use Decision Trees when you need fast, interpretable results and are working with smaller datasets or want to
quickly understand data relationships.
✔
Use Random Forests when you want higher predictive accuracy, can afford longer training times, and are less
concerned about interpretability.
✔
Use a decision tree when interpretability is important, and you need a simple and easy-to-understand model.
✔
Use a random forest when you want better generalization performance, robustness to overfitting, and improved
accuracy, especially on complex datasets with high-dimensional feature spaces.
✔
If computational efficiency is a concern and you have a small dataset, a decision tree might be more
appropriate.
✔
If you have a large dataset with complex relationships between features and labels, a random forest is likely to
provide better results.
38

Computing system whose central theme is borrowed from the
analogy of biological neural networks.

Named as “artificial neural systems,” or “parallel distributed
processing systems,” or “connectionist systems.”

processors which operate in parallel.

native_text:
What is Artificial Neural Network ?
•
Every neuron is connected with other neuron through a connection link.
•
Each connection link is associated with a weight that has information
about the input signal.
•
This is the most useful information for neurons to solve a particular
problem because the weight usually excites or inhibits the signal that is
being communicated.
•
Each neuron has an internal state, which is called an activation signal.
•
Output signals, which are produced after combining the input signals
and activation rule, may be sent to other units.

Soma (cell body)—Sums all the incoming signals to generate
input.
•
Axon—When the sum reaches a threshold value, neuron fires and
the signal travels down the axon to the other neurons.
•
Synapses—The point of interconnection of one neuron with other
neurons. The amount of signal transmitted depend upon the
strength (synaptic weights) of the connections.
•
The connections can be inhibitory (decreasing strength) or
excitatory (increasing strength) in nature.
•
So, neural network, in general, is a highly interconnected network
of billions of neuron with trillion of interconnections between
them.
verbatim_text_span: Biological Neuron • Dendrite—Receives signals from other neurons. • Soma (cell body)—Sums all the incoming signals to generate input. • Axon—When the sum reaches a threshold value, neuron fires and the signal travels down the axon to the other neurons. • Synapses—The point of interconnection of one neuron with other neurons. The amount of signal transmitted depend upon the strength (synaptic weights) of the connections. • The connections can be inhibitory (decreasing strength) or excitatory (increasing strength) in nature. • So, neural network, in general, is a highly interconnected network of billions of neuron with trillion of interconnections between them.

HOW DOES ANN WORKS
❑Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are comprised of a node layers,
containing an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output
layer.
❑Each node, or artificial neuron, connects to another and has an
associated weight and threshold.
❑Once an input layer is determined, weights are assigned. These
weights help determine the importance of any given variable, with
larger ones contributing more significantly to the output compared to
other inputs.
❑Their respective weights and then summed. Afterward, the output is
passed through an activation function, which determines the output
❑If the output of any individual node is above the specified threshold
value, that node is activated, sending data to the next layer of the
network.

How Does ANN Learns?
❑Typically, an ANN is initially trained or fed large amounts of
data. Training consists of providing input and telling the
network what the output should be.
❑For example, to build a network that identifies the faces of
actors, the initial training might be a series of pictures,
including actors, non-actors, masks, statuary and animal
faces.
❑Each input is accompanied by the matching identification,
such as actors' names or "not actor" or "not human"
information. Providing the answers allows the model to
adjust its internal weightings to learn how to do its job better.

native_text:
Learning in Biology(Human)
•
Learning = learning by adaptation
•
The young animal learns that the green fruits are sour, while the
yellowish/reddish ones are sweet. The learning happens by adapting
the fruit picking behaviour.
•
At the neural level the learning happens by changing of the synaptic
strengths, eliminating some synapses, and building new ones.
•
The objective of adapting the responses on the basis of the
information received from the environment is to achieve a better
state. E.g., the animal likes to eat many energy rich, juicy fruits that
make its stomach full, and makes it feel happy.
•
In other words, the objective of learning in biological organisms is to
optimise the number of available resources, happiness, or in general
to achieve a closer to optimal state

Learning principle for
artificial neural networks
•
Learning occurs when the weights inside the network get
updated after many iterations.
•
For example—Suppose we have inputs in the form of
patterns for two different class of patterns—I & 0 as shown
and b -bias and y as desired output.
•
We want to classify input patterns into either pattern ‘I’ &
‘O’.
•
Following are the steps performed:
•
9 inputs from x1—x9 along with bias b (input having weight
value 1) is fed to the network for the first pattern.
•
Initially, weights are initialized to zero.
•
Then weights are updated for each neuron using the
formulae: Δ wi = xi y for i = 1 to 9 (Hebb’s Rule)

●It searches for weight values that minimize the total error
of the network over the set of training examples (training

●Backpropagation consists of the repeated application of
the following twopasses:
– Forward pass: In this step, the network is activated
on one
example and the error of (each neuron of)
the output layer is computed.
– Backward pass: in this step the network error is
used for updating the weights. The error is propagated
backwards from the
output
layer
through
the
network layer by layer. This is done by recursively
computing the local gradient of each neuron.
verbatim_text_span: TrainingAlgorithm: Backpropagation ●It searches for weight values that minimize the total error of the network over the set of training examples (training set). ●Backpropagation consists of the repeated application of the following twopasses: – Forward pass: In this step, the network is activated on one example and the error of (each neuron of) the output layer is computed. – Backward pass: in this step the network error is used for updating the weights. The error is propagated backwards from the output layer through the network layer by layer. This is done by recursively computing the local gradient of each neuron.

native_text:
Introduction
• Clustering or cluster analysis is a machine learning technique, which groups
the unlabelled dataset. It can be defined as "A way of grouping the data
points into different clusters, consisting of similar data points. The
objects with the possible similarities remain in a group that has less or
no similarities with another group.“
• It does it by finding some similar patterns in the unlabelled dataset such as
shape, size, color, behavior, etc., and divides them as per the presence and
absence of those similar patterns.
• It is an unsupervised learning method; hence no supervision is provided to
the algorithm, and it deals with the unlabeled dataset.
• After applying this clustering technique, each cluster or group is provided
with a cluster-ID. ML system can use this id to simplify the processing of
large and complex datasets.
• The clustering technique is commonly used for statistical data analysis.

Clustering Algorithms
●Machine learning datasets may have millions of examples and some
clustering algorithms may not scale efficiently.
●Many clustering algorithms compute the similarity between all pair of
examples. Their runtime increases as the square of the number of
examples n, denoted as O(n2) in complexity notation.
●The O(n2) algorithms are not practical for datasets with millions of
examples.
●The k-means algorithm has a complexity of O(n), which means the
algorithm scales linearly with n.

native_text:
Application of Clustering
1.
In Identification of Cancer Cells: The clustering algorithms are widely used for
the identification of cancerous cells. It divides the cancerous and non-cancerous
data sets into different groups.
2.
In Search Engines: Search engines also work on the clustering technique. The
search result appears based on the closest object to the search query. It does it
by grouping similar data objects in one group that is far from the other dissimilar
objects. The accurate result of a query depends on the quality of the clustering
algorithm used.
3.
Customer Segmentation: It is used in market research to segment the
customers based on their choice and preferences.
4.
In Biology: It is used in the biology stream to classify different species of plants
and animals using the image recognition technique.
5.
In Land Use: The clustering technique is used in identifying the area of similar
lands use in the GIS database. This can be very useful to find that for what
purpose the particular land should be used, that means for which purpose it is
more suitable.

native_text:
Types of Clustering Methods
1.Partitioning Clustering :
• It is a type of clustering that divides the data into non-hierarchical groups. It is
also known as the Centroid-based method. The most common example of
partitioning clustering is the K-Means Clustering algorithm.
• In this type, the dataset is divided into a set of k groups, where K is used to
define the number of pre-defined groups. The cluster center is created in such
a way that the distance between the data points of one cluster is minimum as
compared to another cluster centroid.

clusters in the dataset and connects the areas of high densities into clusters.

• These algorithms can face difficulty in clustering the data points if the dataset
has varying densities and high dimensions.

the Agglomerative Hierarchical algorithm.

• Hierarchical clustering is another unsupervised machine learning algorithm,
which is used to group the unlabeled datasets into a cluster and also known
as hierarchical cluster analysis or HCA.
• In this algorithm, we develop the hierarchy of clusters in the form of a tree,
and this tree-shaped structure is known as the dendrogram.
• Sometimes the results of K-means clustering and hierarchical clustering
may look similar, but they both differ depending on how they work. As there
is no requirement to predetermine the number of clusters as we did in the K-
Means algorithm.
The hierarchical clustering technique has two approaches:
➢Agglomerative: Agglomerative is a bottom-up approach, in which the
algorithm starts with taking all data points as single clusters and merging
them until one cluster is left.
➢Divisive: Divisive algorithm is the reverse of the agglomerative algorithm as
it is a top-down approach.

native_text:
K-Means Clustering
• K-Means Clustering is an Unsupervised Learning algorithm, which groups
the unlabeled dataset into different clusters. Here K defines the number of
pre-defined clusters that need to be created in the process, as if K=2, there
will be two clusters, and for K=3, there will be three clusters, and so on.
• It allows us to cluster the data into different groups and a convenient way to
discover the categories of groups in the unlabeled dataset on its own without
the need for any training.
• It is a centroid-based algorithm, where each cluster is associated with a
centroid. The main aim of this algorithm is to minimize the sum of distances
between the data point and their corresponding clusters.
• The algorithm takes the unlabeled dataset as input, divides the dataset into
k-number of clusters, and repeats the process until it does not find the best
clusters. The value of k should be predetermined in this algorithm.

native_text:
Disadvantage of K-means Clustering
●k must be chosen manually.
●Results depend on initial values. For low k, this dependence can be mitigated
by running k-means several times with different initial values and picking the
best result. As k increases, k-means seeding may needed to pick better initial
centroids.
●Difficulty clustering data of varying size and densities without generalization.
●Difficulty clustering outliers. Centroids can be dragged by outliers, or outliers
might get their own cluster instead of being ignored. Consider removing or
clipping outliers before clustering.
●Difficulty scaling with number of dimensions. As the number of dimension in
the data increases, a distance-based similarity measure converges to a
constant value between any given examples. PCA or spectral clustering can be
used to reduce dimensionality.

clustering, which adds pre-clustering steps to the algorithm. To perform
spectral clustering:
1. Reduce the dimensionality of feature data by using PCA.
2. Project all data points into the lower-dimensional subspace.
3. Cluster the data in this subspace using your chosen algorithm.

Dataset
A dataset is a table of rows of training examples, and columns of attributes. Each row has:
•
A label – the attribute that you want to predict.
•
Features – the attribute that are used as inputs to predict the label.
For the house-price prediction scenario, the features could be:
•
The square footage.
•
The number of bedrooms and bathrooms.
•
The zip code.
The label is the historical house price.
Source: Microsoft

native_text:
Data Cleaning
Data cleaning is the process of identifying and correcting errors or consistencies in the data.
For example:
•
Handling missing values – Mean/Mode imputation, fill in or remove missing data.
•
Removing duplicates – Eliminating duplicate records to ensure each entry is unique and
relevant.
•
Correcting inconsistent formats – Standardizing formats to maintain consistency.

Data integration involves combination data from multiple sources to create a unified dataset.

consistency.

Data deduplication – Identifying and removing duplicate entries across multiple datasets.

Data Transformation
Data transformation converts data into formats suitable for analysis, machine learning, or mining.
For example:
•
Scaling and normalization – Adjusting numeric values to a common scale.
•
Encoding categorical variables – Converting categorical data into numerical values using one-
hot or label encoding techniques.
•
Feature engineering and extraction – Creating new features or selecting important ones to
improve model performance.

native_text:
Data Reduction
Data reduction simplifies the dataset by reducing the number of features or records while
preserving the essential information.
Techniques for data reduction:
•
Feature selection – Choosing the most important features contributing to the model’s
performance.
•
Principal component analysis (PCA) – A dimensionality reduction technique that transforms
data into a lower-dimensional space.
•
Sampling methods – Reducing the size of the dataset by selecting representative samples is
useful for handling large datasets.

Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is used by data scientists to analyse and investigate data sets and summarize
main characteristics.
Three main types of EDA:

Univariate EDA - looking at a single variable at a time.
●
Bivariate EDA - looking at two variables at a time.
●
Multivariate EDA involves looking at three or more variables at a time.

native_text:
Exploratory Data Analysis
Graphical methods consists of creating charts, graphs, and other visualizations to explore the data. Non-
graphical methods involve using statistical techniques to explore the data.
•
Univariate non-graphical: The data analysed consists of just one variable. Since it’s a single variable, it
doesn’t deal with causes or relationships. (mean, median, spread, shape)
•
Univariate graphical: Non-graphical methods don’t provide a full picture of the data. Graphical methods
are needed.
•
Multivariate non-graphical: Relationship between more than two variables of the data through cross-
tabulation or statistics.
•
Multivariate graphical: Uses graphics to display relationships between more than two variables of data.

conclusions.
•
High costs and time investment
Manual labelling data can be labor intensive and costly.

A Supervised Learning Algorithm
A supervised learning algorithm as having two components: a model class and an optimizer.
The model class
●
The model represents a set of possible relationships between BMI and risk that we believe to be true.

Why Supervised Learning?
Supervised learning is a tool that is applicable on tasks such as:
●Predictive modeling. Supervised learning can outperform human experts when more
data are gathered to characterize a patient. For instance, age, gender, historical blood
pressure, medical notes.
●Understanding the mechanisms through which input variables can affect targets. For
example, we inspected the slope of the model and inferred from the data that a high
BMI tends to increase diabetes risk.
Source: https://kuleshov-group.github.io/aml-book/contents/lecture1-introduction.html#supervised-learning

Targets: Regression vs. Classification
Two types of supervised learning problems, regression and classification can be
distinguished based on the form of the target variable:
●Regression: The target variable is continuous. We are fitting a curve in a high-dimensional
feature space that approximates the shape of the dataset.
●Classification: The target variable is discrete. Each discrete value corresponds to a class and
we are looking for a hyperplane that separates the different classes.
Source: https://kuleshov-group.github.io/aml-book/contents/lecture1-introduction.html#supervised-learning

Anatomy of a Supervised Learning Problem:
The Learning Algorithm
The high-level structure of a supervised learning algorithm consisted of three
components:
●A model class is the set of possible models that we consider.
●An objective function defines how good a model is.
●An optimizer finds the best predictive model in the model class according to the objective
function.
Source: https://kuleshov-group.github.io/aml-book/contents/lecture1-introduction.html#supervised-learning

Summary: Components of a Supervised Machine
Learning Problem
●Formally, to apply supervised learning, we define a dataset and a learning algorithm.
Features, Attributes, Targets
Dataset
Learning Algorithm
Predictive Model
Model Class + Objective + Optimizer
●A dataset consists of training examples, which are pairs of inputs and targets. Each input is a
vector of features or attributes. A learning algorithm can be fully defined by a model class,
objective and optimizer.
●The output of a supervised learning is a predictive model that maps inputs to targets. For
instance, it can predict targets on new inputs.
Source: https://kuleshov-group.github.io/aml-book/contents/lecture1-introduction.html#supervised-learning

native_text:
Introduction - What is unsupervised learning?
Unsupervised learning utilizes dataset that does not contain labels.
Unsupervised learning aims to discover interesting and useful patterns in data:
●Clusters of related data points. For example, we might want to discover groups of similar
customers from the logs of an e-commerce website.
●Outliers, i.e., particularly unusual or interesting data points. For example, suspicious financial
transactions.
●Denoised signals. Recovering an image corrupted with white noise.
Source: https://kuleshov-group.github.io/aml-book/contents/lecture8-unsupervised-learning.html#the-language-of-unsupervised-learning

●A model class: the set of possible unsupervised models we consider.
●An objective function, which defines how good a model is.
●An optimizer, which finds the best predictive model in the model class according to the
objective function.

An Example: K-Means
The K-means algorithm is derived to better understand how these three components (model
class, objective function, optimizer) define an unsupervised learning algorithm.
At a high level, K-means performs the following steps. Starting from random centroids, we
repeat until convergence.
1.
Update each cluster: assign each point to its closest centroid.
2.
Set each centroid to be the center of the its cluster.
