native_text:
Detecting Overfitting and Underfitting
In real-life scenarios when data is not in two-dimensional, visualizing the data and the cluster centres
might not help us to detect overfitting or underfitting. We also may not have the access to the true
cluster labels.
Generally, in unsupervised learning, overfitting and underfitting are more difficult to quantify than in
supervised learning due to several reasons:
●Performance may depend on our intuition and require human evaluation.
●If we know the true labels, we can measure the accuracy of the clustering. But we do not have the
labels for unsupervised learning.
If our model is probabilistic, in order to detect overfitting without labels is to compare the log-
likelihood between the training set and a holdout set.
Source: https://kuleshov-group.github.io/aml-book/contents/lecture8-unsupervised-learning.html#the-language-of-unsupervised-learning

The elbow method is a useful heuristic that can be used to tune hyperparameters in unsupervised
learning. E.g., choosing K for K-means. The elbow method works as follows:

●The “elbow” of the curve happens when its rate of decrease substantially slows down.
●The “elbow” is a good guess for the hyperparameter.
When K = 4, the objective value
does not improve too much
anymore.
The decrease in objective values
slows down after K = 4. After

line.

What is model evaluation?
●Model evaluation is the process of utilizing various evaluation metrics to enhance and
assess an ML model’s performance.
●The performance of the model should be accessed not only during the development phase
but also after model deployment phase.
●There are several key metrics that you can use to evaluate your model: (1) accuracy; (2)
Precision; (3) Recall (Sensitivity); (4) F1-score; and (5) ROC-AUC.

Some common benefits of evaluation ML models include:
●Overfitting detection: Evaluating models can help you detect and minimize failures when
you integrate new data into the model.
●Improve model performance: Implementing model evaluation and performance metrics
eagles the model to gain more insight in order to improve its performance.
●Ongoing improvements: You can reevaluate the model after it is deployed. This allows
continuous improvement and model updates.
●Enhanced predictions: After you have evaluated a model, you can use it to make accurate
and reliable predictions based on the data it is trained on.

Common challenges in model evaluation
Model evaluation may also pose some challenges:
●Data dependency: Dependency on reliable data may be a challenge because you must
ensure that you have high-quality, well-labeled data to properly train and evaluate your
ML model.
●Incorrect metric selection: If you choose the wrong metrics when performing model
evaluation, your ML model may develop incorrect outputs.
●Extensive resource allocations: Model evaluation requires various resources, which may
be time-consuming to allocate, and metrics such as cross-validation are very time-
intensive.
●Model drift: This process refers to changes in the distribution of data, which can make the
initial evaluations you made irrelevant and inaccurate.

native_text:
Evaluation metrics: Accuracy
Accuracy is the proportion of all classifications that were correct, whether positive or
negative. It is mathematically defined as:
Accuracy = correct classifications / total classifications = TP + TN / TP + TN + FP + FN
In the spam classification example, accuracy measures the fraction of all emails correctly
classified.
A perfect model would have zero false positives and zero false negatives and therefore an
accuracy of 1.0, or 100%.
Accuracy incorporates all four outcomes from the confusion matrix (TP, FP, TN, FN), given a
balanced dataset, with similar numbers of example in both classes, accuracy can serve as a
coarse-grained measure of model quality.
https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course/classification/accuracy-precision-recall

Evaluation metrics: Recall or true positive rate
The true positive rate (TPR), or proportion of all actual positives that were classified correctly as
positives, is also known as recall.
Recall is mathematically defined as:
Recall (or TPR) = correctly classified actual positives / all actual positives = TP / TP + FN
False negatives are actual positives that were misclassified as negatives. That is why they
appear in the denominator.

Evaluation metrics: False positive rate
The false positive rate (FPR) is the proportion of all actual negatives that were classified
incorrectly as positives, also known as the probability of false alarm. It is mathematically
defined as:
FPR = incorrectly classified actual negatives / all actual negatives = FP / FP + TN
False positives are actual negatives that were misclassified, which is why they appear in the
denominator.
A perfect model would have zero false positives and therefore a FPR of 0.0, which is to say, a
0% false alarm rate.
In a imbalanced dataset, where the number of actual negatives is very, very low, say 1-2
examples in total, FPR is less meaningful and less useful as a metric.
https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course/classification/accuracy-precision-recall

Evaluation metrics: Precision
Precision is the proportion of all the model’s positive classifications that are actually positive. It is
mathematically defined as:
Precision = correctly classified actual positives / everything classified as positive = TP / TP + FP
In the spam classification example, precision measures the fraction of emails classified as spam that
were actually spam.
A hypothetical perfect model would have zero false positives and therefore a precision of 1.0.
In an imbalanced dataset where the number of actual positives is very, very low, say 1-2 examples in
total, precision is less meaningful and less useful as a metric.
Precision improves as false positives decrease, while recall improves when false negatives decrease. As
a result, precision and recall often show an inverse relationship, where improving one of them worsens
the other.
https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course/classification/accuracy-precision-recall

native_text:
Evaluation metrics: F1 score
The F1 score is the harmonic mean (a kind of average) of precision and recall.
Mathematically, it is given by:
F1 = 2 * (precision * recall / precision + recall) = (2TP / 2TP + FP + FN)
This metric balances the importance of precision and recall, and is preferable to accuracy for class-
imbalanced datasets.
When precision and recall both have perfect scores of 1.0, F1 will also have a perfect score of 1.0.
More broadly, when precision and recall are close in values, F1 will be close to their value.
When precision and recall are far apart, F1 will be similar to whichever metric is worse.

●Too-strong regularization, meaning that the model was oversimplified and lost some
necessary complexity.
●Bugs in the model training pipeline.
●The set of features provided to the model being insufficient for the task.

Cross validation
Cross validation is a model assessment technique used to evaluate a machine learning
algorithm’s performance in making predictions on new datasets that it has not been trained
on. This is done by partitioning the known dataset, using a subset to train the algorithm and
the remaining data for testing.
Each round of cross-validation involves randomly partitioning the original dataset into a
training set and a testing set. The training set is then used to train a supervised learning
algorithm and the testing set is used to evaluate its performance. This process is repeated
several times and the average cross-validation error is used as a performance indicator.

native_text:
Distance of loss
For example, if a model predicts 2, but the actual value is 5, we can ignore that the
loss is negative −3 (2 −5 = −3). Instead, we consider that the distance between the
values is 3. Thus, all methods for calculating loss remove the sign.
The most two common methods to remove the sign are the following:
●Take the absolute value of the difference between the actual value and the
prediction.
●Square the difference between the actual value and the prediction.
Source: https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course/linear-regression

native_text:
Gradient descent
Gradient descent is a mathematical technique that iteratively finds the weight and bias that
produce the model with the lowest loss.
The model begins training with randomized weights and biases near zero, and then repeats the
following steps:
1. Calculate the loss with the current weight and bias.
2. Determine the direction to move the weights and bias that reduce loss.
3. Move the weight and bias values a small amount in the direction that reduces loss.
4. Return to step one and repeat the process until the model can’t reduce the loss any further.
Source: https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course/linear-regression

Epochs
●During training, an epoch means that the model has processed every example in the
training set once. For instance, a training set with 1000 examples and a mini-batch size of
100 examples, it will take the model 10 iterations to complete one epoch.
●Training typically requires many epochs and the system needs to process every example in
the training set multiple times.
●The number of epochs is a hyperparameter that you need to set before the model begins
training.
●In many cases, you’ll need to experiment with how many epochs it takes for the model to
converge.
●In general, more epochs produces a better model, but also takes more time to train.
Source: https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course/linear-regression

native_text:
Introduction
•
Naive Bayes is a supervised machine learning algorithm used mainly for classification
tasks.
•
It is based on Bayes' Theorem — a rule that calculates the probability of an event based on prior
knowledge of conditions related to the event.
•
Uses probability to classify data. Picks the class with the higher probability.
•
"Naive": Because it naively assumes feature independence, even though, in reality, features
might be related. (e.g., "win" and "prize" are treated as unrelated).
•
"Bayes": Because it is based on Bayes’ Theorem, developed by mathematician Thomas Bayes.
3

Disadvantages
1. Strong Independence Assumption
∙
Assumes that all features are independent, which is often unrealistic in real-world data.
∙
In practice, predictors are often correlated (e.g., the presence of "snow" and "cold" are
related in text data), violating the independence assumption and possibly leading to
incorrect classifications.
2. Zero Frequency Problem
∙
If a categorical variable value in the test set was not observed in the training data, the model
assigns zero probability to the entire prediction.
∙

operational processes in companies and scientific organizations. In addition,they form the basis for
decisions. Bad data quality can negatively affect decisions and have a negative impact on results.

to as data munging or data crunching,tofind the dirty data and to transform and clean them.The aim

further analysis steps. Only then can knowledge be obtained that may bring added value.This paper

datafromheterogeneous data sourcesduring their acquisition and integration.

visuals to communicate information truthfully, transparently, and
fairly, without misleading the viewer—even unintentionally.

doesn’t mean it’s ethically sound.”

b. Loss of Data Integrity
• Data integrity refers to the accuracy, consistency, and
reliability of data throughout its lifecycle. When data is

slide_or_section_title: How is a Missing Value Represented in a Dataset?
native_text:
How is a Missing Value Represented in a
Dataset?
1.
NaN (Not a Number): In many programming languages and data analysis tools, missing values are
represented as NaN. This is the default for libraries like Pandas in Python.
2.
NULL or None: In databases and some programming languages, missing values are often represented
as NULL or None. For instance, in SQL databases, a missing value is typically recorded as NULL.
3.
Empty Strings: Sometimes, missing values are denoted by empty strings (""). This is common in text-based
data or CSV files where a field might be left blank.
4.
Special Indicators: Datasets might use specific indicators like -999, 9999, or other unlikely values to signify
missing data. This is often seen in older datasets or specific industries where such conventions were
established.
5.
Blanks or Spaces: In some cases, particularly in fixed-width text files, missing values might be represented
by spaces or blank fields.
10

native_text:
Missing Completely At Random (MCAR)
MCAR occurs when the probability of data being missing is uniform
across all observations. There is no relationship between the
missingness of data and any other observed or unobserved data within
the dataset. This type of missing data is purely random and lacks any
discernible pattern.
Example: In a survey about library books, some overdue book values in
the dataset are missing due to human error in recording.
13
verbatim_text_span: Missing Completely At Random (MCAR) MCAR occurs when the probability of data being missing is uniform across all observations. There is no relationship between the missingness of data and any other observed or unobserved data within the dataset. This type of missing data is purely random and lacks any discernible pattern. Example: In a survey about library books, some overdue book values in the dataset are missing due to human error in recording. 13

chunk_id: SAIA2143__Topic 2-Identifying and Handling Missing Data with Spreadsheets-d.pdf__p14
doc_id: Topic 2-Identifying and Handling Missing Data with Spreadsheets-d.pdf
native_text:
Missing At Random (MAR)
MAR data occurs when the probability of data being missing depends
only on the observed data and not on the missing data itself. In other
words, the missingness can be explained by variables for which you
have complete information. There is a pattern in the missing values, but
this pattern can be explained by other observed variables.
Example: In a survey, ‘Age’ values might be missing for those who did
not disclose their ‘Gender’. Here, the missingness of ‘Age’ depends on
‘Gender’, but the missing ‘Age’ values are random among those who
did not disclose their ‘Gender’.
14

In other words, the missingness can be explained by variables for which you have complete information. There is a pattern in the missing values, but this pattern can be explained by other observed variables. Example: In a survey, ‘Age’ values might be missing for those who did not disclose their ‘Gender’. Here, the missingness of ‘Age’ depends on ‘Gender’, but the missing ‘Age’ values are random among those who did not disclose their ‘Gender’. 14

chunk_id: SAIA2143__Topic 2-Identifying and Handling Missing Data with Spreadsheets-d.pdf__p15
doc_id: Topic 2-Identifying and Handling Missing Data with Spreadsheets-d.pdf
native_text:
Missing Not At Random (MNAR)
MNAR occurs when the missingness of data is related to the
unobserved data itself, which is not included in the dataset. This type
of missing data has a specific pattern that cannot be explained by
observed variables.
Example: In a survey about library books, people with more overdue
books might be less likely to respond to the survey. Thus, the number
of overdue books is missing and depends on the number of books
overdue.
15

This type of missing data has a specific pattern that cannot be explained by observed variables. Example: In a survey about library books, people with more overdue books might be less likely to respond to the survey. Thus, the number of overdue books is missing and depends on the number of books overdue. 15

slide_or_section_title: VLOOKUP()- Fill missing values from another dataset
native_text:
VLOOKUP()- Fill missing values from another dataset
Function of VLOOKUP in Excel
VLOOKUP() (Vertical Lookup) is a function in Excel used to search for a value in one column and return a
corresponding value from another column in the same row. It is commonly used to retrieve information
from large datasets, such as product prices, employee details, or student grades.
=VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, [range_lookup])
Arguments:
1. lookup_value – The value you want to search for (e.g., Product ID, Employee ID).
2. table_array – The range of data containing the lookup value and the value to return.
3. col_index_num – The column number (starting from 1) from which to return the result.
4. [range_lookup] – (Optional)
•
TRUE (Approximate match) – If an exact match is not found, it returns the closest lower value.
•
FALSE (Exact match) – Only returns a result if an exact match is found.
56

Example of Duplicate Scenario
We must ensure that we have a single source of truth for each observation. There
are scenarios where we have multiple observations about a single customer, either
because there is a double form submission by the user, or errors were made during
data entry. Regardless of how this comes about, we need to develop a single,
complete version of the truth.
This will help businesses ensure that:
1. Time and money is not wasted targeting the same customer twice.
2. A trusted and complete version of the truth is developed, and reliable business
decisions can be made based on the analysis results.

calculating outliers.

i. Reshaping Data
Changing the structure or layout of a dataset — like rearranging rows and columns —
without changing the data itself.
Common reshaping operations include:
• melt(): Opposite of pivot — it turns multiple columns into rows (makes data longer).
• pivot(): Turn unique values from one column into multiple columns.
• stack(): Compress columns into a new inner row index (makes data taller).
• unstack(): Opposite of stack — moves inner row index back to columns (makes
data wider).
• transpose() (.T): Flip rows and columns — rows become columns and columns
become rows.
• reshape() (mostly using NumPy under the hood): Change the shape of arrays.

native_text:
ii. Chunking with
pd.read_csv(chunksize=...)
• When you load a huge CSV file with Pandas, sometimes it
doesn’t fit in memory (RAM) all at once.
• To handle this, you can read the file in chunks — small
batches of rows — using the chunksize parameter.
• This turns the read operation into an iterator:
Each chunk is a smaller DataFrame you can process one at a
time.

merged = pd.merge(df1, df2, on='id', suffixes=('_df1', '_df2'))

Plagiarism
1.0 PLAGIARISM
(Excerpt from Item 27, UTM Graduate Studies Rules and Regulations)
1.1 Plagiarism in academics includes producing thesis, dissertation, project
report, article, coursework and research findings without acknowledging or
referring to the original sources and claiming as one’s own work. It involves
the submission of the whole or part of the work towards a degree.
1.2 A Student who committed plagiarism will be penalized based upon decision
made by the Faculty Academic Committee.
1.3 Details of prohibition against plagiarism can be referred to UTM Student
Regulations Book.
2.0 EXAMINATION MISCONDUCT
2.1 Students are NOT allowed to do the following during the examination:
a) Give/receive/own any electronic, printed or other forms of information
that is not now allowed during the examinations whether it be inside or
outside the examination hall unless with the permission of the chief
invigilator
b) Make use of the above information to answer the examination questions.
c) Cheating, attempt to cheat or act in manner that is construed as cheating
during an examination.
d) Other misconduct as stated by the university.
3.0 PUNISHMENT
3.1 If a student has acted against the rules and regulations of the examination
and is found guilty by the Faculty Examination Committee, the Senate can
take any of the following actions:
a) Give a mark of ZERO (0) for the course (including coursework); or
b) A mark of ZERO (0) for all the courses registered in that semester.
Students who have found to act against the rules and regulations of the examinations
for the second time will be dealt according to the Universities and Colleges Act, 1971,
Procedures according to the University Technology Malaysia (Students Code of

Description: This dataset contains real-time weather and air quality data from 211 different
countries.
1. Location & Time
These columns tell us where and when the weather data was recorded.
•
country: The name of the country (e.g., "Malaysia", "Japan", "USA").
•
location_name: The specific city or region within that country (e.g., "Kuala Lumpur",
"Tokyo").
•
latitude: The geographic coordinate specifying North/South location.
•
longitude: The geographic coordinate specifying East/West location.
•
timezone: The local time zone of the location (e.g., "Asia/Kuala_Lumpur").
•
last_updated: The exact date and time the weather was recorded (YYYY-MM-DD
HH:MM).
•
last_updated_epoch: The time recorded in "Unix format" (total seconds since Jan 1,
1970). Mainly used by computers for sorting.
2. Temperature & Weather Condition
These columns describe how hot/cold it is and what the sky looks like.
•
temperature_celsius: The current air temperature in degrees Celsius (°C).
•
temperature_fahrenheit: The current air temperature in degrees Fahrenheit (°F).
•
feels_like_celsius: The "Real Feel" temperature. This accounts for humidity and
wind (e.g., it might be 30°C but "feel like" 35°C due to humidity).
•
feels_like_fahrenheit: The "Real Feel" temperature in Fahrenheit.
•
condition_text: A text description of the weather (e.g., "Sunny", "Partly Cloudy",
"Heavy Rain").
•
uv_index: A number from 1-11+ measuring the strength of sunburn-causing
ultraviolet radiation.
o
1-2 (Low), 11+ (Extreme).
3. Wind & Atmosphere
These columns describe the movement of air and storm conditions.
•
wind_kph: Wind speed in Kilometers per Hour (km/h).
•
wind_mph: Wind speed in Miles per Hour (mph).
•
wind_degree: The direction the wind is coming from, measured in degrees (0° =
North, 90° = East).
•
wind_direction: The compass direction of the wind (e.g., "N", "SW", "ENE").
•
gust_kph: The speed of sudden, brief bursts of wind (gusts) in km/h.
•
gust_mph: The speed of wind gusts in mph.
•
pressure_mb: Atmospheric pressure in millibars. Lower pressure often indicates a
storm is coming.
•
pressure_in: Atmospheric pressure in inches of mercury (standard US
measurement).

SAIA 2143
4. Rain, Visibility & Clouds
These columns describe moisture and clarity.
- 9 -
•
precip_mm: The amount of precipitation (rain/snow) that has fallen recently, in
millimeters.
•
precip_in: The amount of precipitation in inches.
•
humidity: The percentage (%) of moisture in the air. 100% usually means rain or fog.
•
cloud: Cloud cover percentage (0% = Clear Sky, 100% = Totally Overcast).
•
visibility_km: How far you can see clearly, in kilometers. Lower numbers mean fog
or haze.
•
visibility_miles: How far you can see clearly, in miles.
5. Air Quality (Pollution)
These columns measure pollutants in the air. Higher numbers = Worse air quality.
•
air_quality_PM2.5: Tiny particles (dust/smoke) small enough to enter the lungs. This
is a key measure of pollution.
•
air_quality_PM10: Larger dust/smoke particles.
•
air_quality_Carbon_Monoxide: Level of CO gas (often from cars/exhaust).
•
air_quality_Ozone: Level of Ozone gas (O3).
•
air_quality_Nitrogen_dioxide: Level of NO2 (often from burning fuel).
•
air_quality_Sulphur_dioxide: Level of SO2 (often from factories).
•
air_quality_us-epa-index: A summary score from 1 (Good) to 6 (Hazardous) used
by the US EPA.
•
air_quality_gb-defra-index: A summary score from 1 (Low) to 10 (Very High) used
by the UK government.
6. Astronomy (Sun & Moon)
These columns track the cycle of the day and night.
•
sunrise: The time the sun rises (e.g., "06:30 AM").
•
sunset: The time the sun sets (e.g., "07:15 PM").
•
moonrise: The time the moon rises.
•
moonset: The time the moon sets.
•
moon_phase: The shape of the moon (e.g., "Full Moon", "Waxing Crescent").
moon_illumination: The percentage of the moon's face that is lit up (0% = New Moon,
100% = Full Moon).
